transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I finally agreed to come in because I just don’t care about the things that usually keep me balanced. Sailing races, my Saturday shift at the historical society, even working in my woodshop—they all feel like chores now. I keep putting them off.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah. It’s not overwhelming, exactly, but there’s this low-grade dread and guilt that follows me around. I keep thinking I should have seen one more risk coming, even though people tell me the controls were in place.
Did these feelings start after a specific stressful event?
Yeah. It started after the scaffold accident during the business readjustment. That was a little over a year ago now.
Have you felt this low or down most days for the past two years?
No, not two years. It started after the scaffold accident, so it’s been a little over a year.
Do these feelings still seem mainly connected to the scaffold accident and its aftermath?
Yes. It’s tied to that accident—the feeling that I should’ve caught one more risk, even though everyone says the controls were in place. The dread and guilt have kind of stayed with me.
Before the scaffold accident, had you ever gone through a period of depression like this?
I’m not sure. I can’t really think of a time before this that felt like what I’ve been dealing with lately.
Have these feelings continued for more than six months after the accident and its immediate aftermath ended?
Yes. It’s been continuing since the scaffold accident during the business readjustment—over a year now.
Since this started, have you had trouble sleeping?

Most nights I get to bed okay, but then I wake up around two or three. My mind goes right back to that job site, and I just lie there listening to every little sound instead of really getting back to sleep.
Since this started, have you noticed a big change in your appetite?
I haven’t really noticed a big change in my appetite, no.
Since this started, have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes, at times. Out of nowhere I’ll picture that scaffold dropping, especially if I hear metal clank or a backup alarm. For a few minutes it’s hard to stay focused on the meeting or conversation I’m in.
Since the accident, have you been feeling anxious or on edge?
Yeah, I guess so. There’s this low-grade dread that’s kind of always there, and guilt too—like I should’ve seen one more risk coming, even though everyone tells me the controls were in place.
Since the scaffold accident, have you been avoiding reminders of it?

Yeah. I’ve gotten pretty good at routing my day so I don’t have to go near that coastal site or the harbor walkways by the cranes. And if someone starts going over what happened, I usually try to steer clear of that conversation too.
Since the accident, have you been blaming yourself for what happened?
Yeah. I keep thinking I should’ve caught one more risk somehow. People tell me the controls were in place, but I still carry this guilt around, along with this constant low-level dread.
Since the accident, have you been feeling jumpy or easily startled?
Yeah. If a metal ladder gets dropped or a truck gate slams, I jump really hard before I can stop myself. Then my heart stays racing longer than it feels like it should.
During the scaffold accident, did anyone die or get seriously injured?
I’m not sure—I don’t really know what happened to everyone afterward.
Were you there in person when the scaffold accident happened?
I’m not sure what you mean by “there in person.” I don’t really know how to answer that.
When the scaffold accident happened, did you actually see it happen with your own eyes?
I... I’m not sure. I don’t know whether I actually saw it happen or not.
After the scaffold accident, were you the person who had to inspect the scene in person?
I remember walking around the site afterward, but right when the scaffold gave way, there’s a gap. I can’t put that part in order, even after going over it so many times.
When the scaffold gave way, did you feel intense fear or horror?

I don’t know if I’d call it horror in that exact moment. But since then, there’s been this constant low-level dread, and guilt—like I should’ve noticed one more risk, even though everyone says the controls were in place.
At the moment the scaffold gave way, were you physically at the site?
I think I was, but I can’t say for certain. I remember being around the site before and then walking it afterward, but the part right when it gave way is just... missing or out of order for me.
